results.result: The opioid crisis has significantly impacted pregnant women, with OUD prevalence increasing 333% from 1999-2014 and NOWS increasing from 1.2 to 5.8 per 1000 hospital births from 2000-2012, with some regions reaching 33 cases per 1000.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3 are supported by appropriate citations to epidemiological studies (Haight et al., 2018; Ko et al., 2016; Patrick et al., 2015). These claims establish the clinical context and public health significance of the research problem.

results.result: Opioid maintenance therapies (methadone and buprenorphine) represent first-line treatments for pregnant women with OUD because they benefit maternal-fetal outcomes at parturition.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C5 are supported by citation to clinical guidelines (ACOG, 2017). This establishes the standard of care and justifies the use of methadone in the experimental model.

results.result: Prenatal opioid exposure is associated with smaller head circumferences, lower brain volumes, and deficits in white matter microstructure, though existing studies are limited by small sample sizes.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C9 are supported by citations to multiple studies (Towers et al., 2019; Hartwell et al., 2020; Sirnes et al., 2017; Monnelly et al., 2018). The authors appropriately acknowledge the limitation of small sample sizes in prior work, which motivates their own study.

results.result: A large study using ABCD data found reduced motor cortical volumes and surface area in children with prenatal opioid exposure, with effects remaining significant after controlling for confounders, suggesting specific disruption of motor cortex development.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C12 are supported by citation to Hartwell et al., 2020. The inference in C12 about specific disruption of motor cortex development is reasonable given the controlled analysis, though it remains correlational.

results.result: Prior studies revealed poorer motor performance in children exposed to opioids prenatally, suggesting long-lasting changes in motor behavior and associated brain regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C14 are supported by citations to Lee et al., 2020 and Yeoh et al., 2019. The inference in C14 is reasonable but represents a hypothesis rather than established fact.

results.result: Clinical studies on prenatal opioid exposure are complicated by environmental variations (prenatal care, additional substance exposures) that impact neurodevelopmental outcomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C16 are supported by citation to Larson et al., 2019. This establishes the rationale for controlled animal studies.

results.result: Animal models have demonstrated sensorimotor deficits following prenatal opioid exposure, but the underlying mechanisms remain unclear.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C18 are supported by citations to multiple animal studies (Kunko et al., 1996; Robinson et al., 2020; Wallin et al., 2019). This identifies a knowledge gap that the current study addresses.

results.result: Preclinical studies suggest prenatal opioid exposure may prevent normal neuronal development and disturb myelination, which could underlie aberrant neurobehavioral development.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C21 are supported by citations (Lu et al., 2012; Ricalde and Hammer, 1990; Jantzie et al., 2020). Claim C21 is appropriately speculative about the mechanistic link.

results.result: Existing rodent models have limited translational value because they often initiate opioid exposure mid-gestation or later and use morphine rather than methadone/buprenorphine, overlooking effects on early embryonic development.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C26 identify critical limitations in existing models and are supported by citations (Byrnes and Vassoler, 2018; Duffy et al., 2018; Larson et al., 2019). This establishes the need for improved models.

results.result: The study developed a translational mouse model resembling typical human opioid use patterns: oxycodone dependence, transition to methadone maintenance, then pregnancy while maintained on methadone.
results.evaluation: Claim C27 describes the experimental model developed in this study. The model design is clearly described in the methods and represents a novel contribution addressing limitations of prior models.

results.result: PME reduces physical growth persisting into adolescence, disrupts locomotor activity and USV development during preweaning, delays sensorimotor milestones, and alters layer 5 motor cortical neuron properties and connectivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C32 summarize the main findings of the study. These are supported by extensive experimental data presented in Figures 4-9 with appropriate statistical analyses. The claims represent the core results of the manuscript.

results.result: Opioid treatment did not affect pregnancy rates, obstructed labor, litter sizes, or total neonatal deaths.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C36 are supported by statistical analyses (chi-square and t-tests) with non-significant p-values. These findings indicate the model does not grossly impair reproductive outcomes.

results.result: There was a trend for fewer PME males surviving to P7, likely due to greater postnatal deaths in males relative to females in PME litters, rather than differences in sex ratios at birth.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C40 are supported by statistical analyses. The inference in C39 is reasonable given that sex ratios at birth were similar (C38) but male postnatal deaths were higher (C40, p=0.03).

results.result: Methadone levels were highest at G18 in maternal brain (248.9±54.1 ng/g) and plasma (63.5±11.3 ng/mL), accumulated in brain relative to plasma, and the placenta retained high levels of methadone and EDDP. Fetal brain methadone (2100.8±237.6 ng/g) was substantially higher than maternal brain, but dropped precipitously after birth.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C49 are supported by HPLC-MS/MS measurements presented in Figure 2 and Supplementary file 1. The data demonstrate substantial fetal brain exposure and rapid postnatal clearance, which is critical for interpreting behavioral findings.

results.result: Placental methadone levels predicted fetal brain levels at G18 (R²=0.39, p<0.0078), and offspring plasma predicted brain levels at P1 (R²=0.45, p<0.0084) but not P7 (R²=0.008, p=0.74).
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C52 are supported by regression analyses shown in Figure 2c-e. The predictive relationship at G18 and P1 but not P7 is statistically significant and suggests the placenta may serve as a biomarker for fetal exposure.

results.result: Opioid treatment did not affect maternal weights but significantly increased food consumption during the postnatal period, reaching significance at postnatal week 2.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C54 are supported by rmANOVA analyses shown in Figure 3a-b. The increased food consumption may reflect metabolic effects of methadone or compensatory feeding.

results.result: Opioid-treated dams showed no differences in nest quality, pup retrieval latency, or placentophagy compared to controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C57 are supported by statistical analyses (Mann-Whitney tests) and observational data shown in Figure 3c-d. These findings suggest maternal care behavior was grossly intact.

results.result: Oxycodone treatment induced opioid dependency, and methadone maintained this dependency as evidenced by naloxone-precipitated withdrawal behaviors.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C59 are supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3e with significant ANOVA results (p<0.0001). This validates that the dosing protocol produced opioid dependence in dams.

results.result: PME significantly reduced offspring weights and weight gain during preweaning, with reduced body weight persisting into adolescence (P35, P49) across sexes. Body length was also reduced.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C63 are supported by rmANOVA analyses shown in Figure 4a-b with significant main effects of exposure. The persistent growth deficit is a major finding with potential clinical relevance.

results.result: Femur length was unaffected at P7, but whole bone volume tended to be lower (p=0.072). By P35, all structural bone measures were similar between exposure groups.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C70 are supported by statistical analyses shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1. The trend at P7 (C66) did not reach significance, and by P35 differences had resolved, suggesting transient effects on bone development.

results.result: PME did not affect timing of eye opening, ear positioning, or tooth eruption, indicating normal postnatal craniofacial development in this model.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C75 are supported by statistical analyses shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2. The inference in C75 is reasonable given the lack of effects on multiple craniofacial milestones.

results.result: PME offspring displayed relative hyperthermia and increased twitches/jerks at P1, reminiscent of myoclonic jerks in human NOWS, suggesting offspring may experience opioid withdrawal.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C79 are supported by statistical analyses shown in Figure 5a-b. The inference in C79 about withdrawal is reasonable given the rapid drop in brain methadone levels (C48-C49) and similarity to human NOWS symptoms (C78), though direct confirmation would require additional measures.

results.result: Locomotor activity was significantly altered in PME offspring, with reduced activity at P1 (likely due to poor coordination/falling) but greater activity at P7 and P21.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C84 are supported by rmANOVA and post-hoc analyses shown in Figure 5c and Figure 5—figure supplement 1. The inference about poor coordination (C83) is supported by video analysis showing increased falling.

results.result: PME offspring exhibited significantly more vertical jumps at P21, indicating a hyperactive phenotype similar to that reported in opioid-exposed children.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C86 are supported by statistical analysis (Mann-Whitney test, p<0.0001) shown in Figure 5d and comparison with clinical literature (Azuine et al., 2019; Sundelin Wahlsten and Sarman, 2013).

results.result: PME affected thigmotaxis at P7 and reduced grooming and unsupported rearing at P21, likely reflecting increased locomotion rather than anxiolysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C91 are supported by statistical analyses shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2. The interpretation in C89 and C91 that these reflect hyperactivity rather than reduced anxiety is reasonable given the context of other behavioral findings.

results.result: USV production was significantly altered by PME, with female PME offspring vocalizing more than PSE offspring at P7. When collapsed on sex, vocalizations were reduced at P1 and increased at P7.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C99 are supported by rmANOVA and post-hoc analyses shown in Figure 5e and Figure 5—figure supplement 3. The sex-specific effects (C95-C99) are appropriately analyzed and interpreted.

results.result: Total activity correlated with total USV calls at P7 (r=0.41, p=0.0028), suggesting a relationship between hyperactivity and hyper-vocalizations. PME increased specific call types and altered call transition syntax.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C103 are supported by correlation analysis and call classification shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4. The inference in C101 is reasonable given the significant correlation, though causality cannot be determined.

results.result: PME delayed acquisition of surface righting, forelimb grasp, and cliff aversion, but not pivoting or negative geotaxis, indicating impaired ability to produce complex, coordinated motor behaviors in response to multimodal sensory input.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C109 are supported by statistical analyses shown in Figure 5f. The inference in C109 is reasonable given the pattern of deficits in complex sensorimotor tasks but not basic locomotion.

results.result: PME did not alter acoustic startle response or prepulse inhibition in P28-P29 offspring, suggesting sensorimotor gating is intact in this model.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C112 are supported by rmANOVA analyses shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5. The lack of PPI deficits distinguishes this model from prenatal THC exposure (C110).

results.result: No significant differences in brain region volumes were found by MRI, suggesting gross gray matter structure is mostly unaffected by PME.
results.evaluation: Claim C113 is supported by statistical analyses of MRI data shown in Figure 6 and Supplementary file 2. This negative finding is important as it suggests effects are at the cellular/circuit level rather than gross structural level.

results.result: In M1, Cux1+ cell distributions were unchanged, but NeuN densities were significantly reduced in layers 2/3-4 specifically in PME females, while layer 5 was unaffected.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C116 are supported by ANOVA analyses of immunostaining data shown in Figure 7a-e. The sex-specific effect in C115 (p=0.0098 for females) is a notable finding requiring further investigation.

results.result: In ACC, there was a minor but significant Exposure x Bin interaction for Cux1+ and NeuN+ cell densities, with an apparent increase in NeuN+ cells at the layer 5/6 border (p=0.050).
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C118 are supported by rmANOVA analyses shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1. The effect at the layer 5/6 border (C118) is marginal (p=0.050) and should be interpreted cautiously.

results.result: In S1, Cux1 distributions were unchanged, but there was a complex three-way interaction for NeuN+ densities. Overall, there are subtle disruptions in cortical lamination in PME for ACC, S1, and M1, with notable reduction in M1 upper layer neuronal density in females.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C121 are supported by rmANOVA analyses shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2. The inference in C121 appropriately summarizes the pattern of subtle but significant effects across cortical regions.

results.result: L5 M1 neurons from PME mice displayed significantly reduced firing rates in response to injected current, suggesting reduced intrinsic excitability at higher currents, though no post-hoc tests reached significance.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C123 are based on rmANOVA showing a significant interaction (p=0.047) shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1b, but the lack of significant post-hoc tests (C123) weakens the interpretation. The effect may be real but subtle, requiring larger sample sizes or additional validation.

results.result: PME neurons exhibited significantly reduced input resistance, indicating current was translated into smaller voltage changes across the membrane.
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C125 are supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 8d and Supplementary file 3. The inference in C125 correctly interprets the functional consequence of reduced input resistance.

results.result: L5 M1 neurons showed prominent voltage sag and overshoot characteristic of HCN channel Ih expression, with both measures larger in PME mice (though overshoot did not quite reach significance).
results.evaluation: Claims C126-C127 are supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 8c,e,f and citation to Sheets et al., 2011. The voltage sag effect is significant (p=0.027), while overshoot is marginal (p=0.057).

results.result: PME modified the amplitude of local inputs onto layer 5 M1 neurons, with a significant Row x Exposure interaction and increased excitatory responses from L2/3 stimulation, suggesting enhanced L2/3→L5 local pathway.
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C131 are supported by laser scanning photostimulation data shown in Figure 8g-n with significant rmANOVA interaction (p=0.0021). The inference in C131 about enhanced L2/3→L5 pathway is reasonable given the spatial pattern of increased responses.

results.result: Morphology of layer 5 M1 neurons in PME mice is unchanged from PSE littermates, with no differences in dendritic intersections or length by Sholl analysis.
results.evaluation: Claim C132 is supported by Sholl analyses shown in Figure 9c,f with non-significant effects of exposure. This negative finding is important as it suggests functional changes occur without gross morphological alterations.

results.result: This study adds to limited preclinical work by providing the first longitudinal assessment of behavioral and neuronal development in PME offspring with comprehensive characterization including opioid levels, revealing disruptions persisting beyond the neonatal period.
results.evaluation: Claims C133-C137 appropriately summarize the study's contributions and are supported by the comprehensive experimental data presented. The findings do support clinical studies suggesting adverse developmental outcomes (C137).

results.result: The methadone dose was likely in the clinical range and produced opioid dependency in dams. Methadone accumulated in the placenta, and placental levels may predict fetal brain exposure.
results.evaluation: Claims C138-C141 are supported by citations (Devidze et al., 2008; Dryden et al., 2009; Kongstorp et al., 2019) and experimental data. The inference in C141 about predictive value is supported by the regression analysis (C50).

results.result: The increase in fetal brain methadone may result from reduced metabolism, as EDDP was lower and cytochrome P450 expression is dramatically lower prenatally. Nevertheless, methadone was present at pharmacologically relevant levels and likely contributed to aberrant neurobehavioral development.
results.evaluation: Claims C142-C146 are supported by EDDP data, citations (Eap et al., 2002; Hart et al., 2009), and methadone level measurements. The speculation in C142 is reasonable, and the inference in C146 is well-supported by the correlation between exposure and behavioral outcomes.

results.result: The persistent size reduction in PME offspring is consistent with other models and human studies. Possible mechanisms include delayed suckling reflex acquisition or disruption of the hypothalamic-pituitary-somatotropic axis, though effects on growth-related hormones remain unstudied.
results.evaluation: Claims C147-C153 appropriately discuss the growth phenotype with supporting citations. The speculations in C149-C150 are reasonable hypotheses, and C153 correctly identifies a knowledge gap for future work.

results.result: USV production depends on the endogenous opioid system, with MOR agonists reducing USV rates. PME reduces MOR-binding affinity and alters downstream signaling, suggesting USV differences resulted from changes in the endogenous opioid system.
results.evaluation: Claims C154-C159 are supported by citations (Ehret, 2005; Carden et al., 1991; Moles et al., 2004; Kongstorp et al., 2020a). The inference in C159 is reasonable given the known role of MORs in USV production and evidence of altered MOR function in PME.

results.result: The hyperarousal phenotype may represent an enduring consequence of PME on neurocircuitry controlling stress/sensorimotor activity, supporting clinical findings of increased ADHD risk and hyperactivity in opioid-exposed children.
results.evaluation: Claims C160-C162 appropriately interpret the behavioral findings with supporting citations (Azuine et al., 2019; Ornoy et al., 2001; Sundelin Wahlsten and Sarman, 2013; Lee et al., 2020; Yeoh et al., 2019). The speculation in C160 is reasonable given the data.

results.result: Other animal models reported delayed sensorimotor milestones, but reports differ in which specific milestones are affected. For example, negative geotaxis was disrupted in other models but not in this PME model.
results.evaluation: Claims C163-C165 appropriately compare findings with prior work (Kunko et al., 1996; Robinson et al., 2020; Wallin et al., 2019) and acknowledge differences between models.

results.result: Altered M1 L5 pyramidal neuron intrinsic properties may be mediated by enhanced HCN channel-driven Ih, which would narrow spatial and temporal integration windows. PME enhanced the L2/3→L5 pathway, possibly through compensatory mechanisms. HCN channels may represent a therapeutic target.
results.evaluation: Claims C166-C173 provide a mechanistic interpretation supported by electrophysiology data and citations (Berger et al., 2001; Magee, 1998; Stuart and Spruston, 1998; Anderson et al., 2010; Sheets et al., 2011; Weiler et al., 2008). The speculation in C172-C173 is reasonable but requires further validation.

results.result: Methadone inhibits NMDA receptors, which mediate experience-dependent synaptic pruning. PME-induced changes to dendritic pruning may contribute to altered local circuits, potentially mediated by changes to HCN expression or function.
results.evaluation: Claims C174-C176 are supported by citations (Eap et al., 2002; Yu et al., 2013). The speculation in C176 is reasonable but represents a hypothesis requiring further testing.

results.result: Morphological measurements were highly variable, indicating neurons analyzed were a heterogeneous population of thick-tufted neurons.
results.evaluation: Claim C177 appropriately interprets the morphological data variability and acknowledges a limitation of the analysis.

results.result: Clinical evidence supports opioid maintenance therapy for improving pregnancy outcomes, so findings of impaired offspring outcomes should not be interpreted as evidence against such therapies. Instead, early intervention programs may be needed.
results.evaluation: Claims C178-C180 appropriately contextualize the findings with citation to clinical guidelines (ACOG, 2017) and suggest a reasonable clinical implication.

results.result: While prior reports indicated opioid treatment alters maternal behavior, this study and others found no differences in maternal care, suggesting offspring differences result from passive methadone exposure. However, subtle differences in maternal behavior cannot be ruled out.
results.evaluation: Claims C181-C184 appropriately discuss maternal behavior with supporting citations (Slamberová et al., 2001; Wallin et al., 2019; Alipio et al., 2021; Kongstorp et al., 2020b; Tan et al., 2015) and acknowledge limitations.

results.result: Few sex-specific effects were discovered, possibly due to the age at testing or inadequate power to detect subtle differences.
results.evaluation: Claims C185-C186 appropriately acknowledge the limited sex differences and potential reasons, representing honest reporting of findings.

results.result: The study used noncontingent treatment via twice-daily injections, which reduces variability but could interact with injection stress to produce differential outcomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C187-C189 describe the methodological approach and appropriately acknowledge a potential limitation regarding stress effects.

results.result: The model choice was based on epidemiological trends supporting high methadone usage, though numerous variations in human opioid use during pregnancy are not reflected in the model.
results.evaluation: Claims C190-C192 justify the model choice with citation (Duffy et al., 2018) and appropriately acknowledge limitations in capturing the full complexity of human prenatal opioid exposure.

results.result: Differences between rodent and human gestational development are inherent limitations. Findings were collected in preweaning and early adolescent periods; future studies will examine persistence into adulthood.
results.evaluation: Claims C193-C196 appropriately acknowledge inherent limitations of the model and describe the temporal scope of the current study with plans for future work.
